text: In 1905 Peterssen redrew the Norwegian lion for the national coat of arms, and the royal house still uses his version. He grew up in the Hegdehaugen district of Christiania, now Oslo. Study took him to Copenhagen, Karlsruhe, Weimar and Munich, where Franz von Lenbach was among his teachers. His history painting of Christian II signing a death warrant brought early recognition. Later he painted portraits of Henrik Ibsen and Edvard Grieg, and he joined the Skagen Painters.

Gierymski painted a sunlit garden party lit from behind before he had ever been to Paris. The picture, In the Arbour, can be compared with French Impressionism. He was born in Warsaw, the younger brother of the painter Maksymilian Gierymski, and graduated from the Munich academy with a gold medal. In Rome he made Roman Inn and Morra Game, which critics in Warsaw noticed in 1875. He died in Rome in 1901.

Corneille de Lyon never signed or dated a painting, so the first work firmly traced to him was identified only in 1962. He was born in The Hague, which is why he is also called Corneille de La Haye. From 1533 he worked in Lyon, painting portraits on wood panels, some hardly bigger than a postcard. The flesh is thin and the greenish background is thicker. Many other artists worked in the same style, so works are credited to him on quality alone. The Louvre and the Metropolitan Museum are good places to see them.

People knew Franz Krüger as Pferde-Krüger, Horse Krüger. A friendship with the ornithologist Johann Friedrich Naumann, a neighbour in Anhalt, led him to animal painting. He drew horses in the Prussian royal stables and showed his military and hunting pictures at the Berlin academy in 1818. Parades and hundreds of portraits made him the most in-demand military and portrait painter in the city. He became a Royal Professor in 1825 and met Eugène Delacroix in Paris in 1846.

Alessandro Bonvicino went by Moretto, which means the Moor of Brescia. He worked mostly in his home city and painted altarpieces for churches there and in nearby towns. Many are still in the churches they were made for. His full-length Portrait of a Man, dated 1526 and now in the National Gallery in London, seems to be the earliest independent full-length portrait in Italy. The sitter leans on a column in front of a closed-off view of the outdoors. His main assistant, Giovanni Battista Moroni, took up the format.

As a young man in Venice, Sebastiano Luciani was a successful lutenist before he turned to painting. He trained with Giovanni Bellini and Giorgione, then left for Rome in 1511. In 1531 he became Keeper of the Seal to the pope, and the title gave him his nickname, del Piombo. The job meant taking holy orders as a friar, even though he had a wife and two children. Michelangelo and Ariosto called him Fra Bastiano. He painted much less after that, mostly portraits.

Philips Koninck bought a barge line that ran from Amsterdam to Rotterdam, and his boats travelled through the kind of country he painted. He learned to paint from his brother Jacob in Rotterdam. Houbraken, the Dutch writer on art, says he finished his training in Rembrandt's studio. In the late 1640s he began painting panoramas, with a canvas cut across the middle into equal parts of earth and sky. Rembrandt's etching The Goldweigher's Field affected him strongly. He moved to Amsterdam after his second marriage.

Emperor Maximilian I kept a team of artists busy with woodcut books that promoted himself, and Leonhard Beck was one of them. He drew 77 of the 118 illustrations in the poem Theuerdank. When Maximilian demanded a second edition in 1519, Beck revised many of them, though his style clashed with the more skilled artists he was correcting. He also designed 126 blocks for Der Weisskunig. Before that he had helped his father, a miniaturist in Augsburg, with two psalters, and had assisted Hans Holbein the Elder on an altarpiece.

Zick's training began on scaffolds. His father Johannes Zick, a fresco painter, taught him in Munich, and in 1744 his younger brother fell to his death from a scaffold in Weingarten. After a bricklaying apprenticeship he worked with his father for the prince-bishops of Würzburg and Speyer. A stay in Paris in 1756 widened his circle. Four years later he painted frescoes at Schloss Engers and became court painter to the Elector of Trier. After 1774 he also designed inlaid pictures for the cabinet maker David Roentgen.

Ramsay's full-length portrait of the Duke of Argyll was later printed on Royal Bank of Scotland banknotes. He was the eldest son of the poet Allan Ramsay. In London he trained under Hans Hysing, then left in 1736 for Rome, where he worked for three years under Francesco Solimena. Back in Edinburgh in 1738, he drew attention with a head of Duncan Forbes of Culloden. He later moved to London. In 1752 he married Margaret Lindsay, a drawing pupil, after the two had eloped.

Cazin was the son of a well-known doctor from Samer in Pas-de-Calais. After training in France he went to England, where the Pre-Raphaelites left a strong mark on him. His early pictures were religious, including The Flight into Egypt. Later he set figures in luminous landscapes and became a leader of a new school of idealistic subject painting. His wife Marie was his pupil, and she exhibited her first picture at the Salon in 1876, the same year in which Cazin himself made his debut there. He also worked as a ceramicist and museum curator.

Le Sueur spent his whole life in Paris. His father was a turner and wood sculptor who placed him with Vouet. Some paintings made for the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili were woven as tapestries and brought him notice. He then decorated the mansion of Lambert de Thorigny, though other commissions kept interrupting and he left the job unfinished. In 1648 he helped found the French Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture and was one of its original twelve elders. He is known mostly for religious subjects.

Leibl's father directed the cathedral choir in Cologne, but the son was first apprenticed to a locksmith. He began his training as a painter in 1861 and entered the Munich Academy three years later. A visit by Gustave Courbet pushed local artists toward loose painting straight from nature. In 1869 Leibl went to Paris and met Manet, and then the Franco-Prussian War sent him home. He left Munich for the Bavarian countryside and painted peasants without any sentiment. His best known picture, Three Women in Church, hangs in Hamburg.

Jarvis's great, great uncle was the Methodist leader John Wesley. He was born in South Shields, England, and his father, a mariner, moved the family to Philadelphia in the mid-1780s. He apprenticed to Edward Savage around 1796 and followed him to New York in 1801. Thomas Sully and Henry Inman worked as his assistants. In New Orleans he painted a portrait of Andrew Jackson, who was then a general, and he kept up the odd dress and manners he was known for.

Wen Zhengming was two years old when his father passed the top imperial examination and left for a post in Zhejiang. In 1489 he began studying under Shen Zhou, who founded the Wu school of painting. Wen later became a leading figure of that school and is counted among the Four Masters of Ming painting. A friend of the family built the Humble Administrator's Garden. Wen painted two albums of its views and wrote poems about it. His sons and a nephew became artists too.

Allori's father died in 1541, and the painter Bronzino, a close friend of the family, raised him and taught him. He sometimes used the name Bronzino himself, and so did his son Cristofano. To learn anatomy he dissected human bodies supplied by a hospital. For the Studiolo of Francesco I he painted four panels, among them a Banquet of Cleopatra and a scene of pearl divers. Later, at Poggio a Caiano, he expanded a fresco that Andrea del Sarto had painted decades before.

Sellaio's nickname comes from his father's trade, saddle making. According to Vasari he trained with Fra Filippo Lippi, where he would have met Botticelli, who left a lasting mark on his work. He joined the painters' confraternity in Florence in 1460. In 1473 he formed a partnership with Filippo di Giuliano that lasted until his death. Today he is best known for paintings on the fronts of cassoni, the wedding chests. These often show stories from ancient mythology, Roman history or the Bible.

Cotes set up his business in his father's apothecary premises on Cork Street in London, and the chemistry he picked up there helped him make pastels. He admired Rosalba Carriera and worked mostly in pastel and crayon at first. Later he turned to oils and painted them thinly, in imitation of his pastel technique. Peter Toms, a specialist drapery painter, did the costumes in many of his pictures. He painted The Young Cricketer. In 1768 he co-founded the Royal Academy.

Peder Als sold a painting of a biblical subject to the King of Denmark in 1743, and people took notice. He studied under Carl Gustaf Pilo and won the academy's gold medal in 1755. A trip to Rome and Paris followed. In Rome he spent most of his time copying Raphael and Andrea del Sarto. His colouring was thought too sombre for portraits of women. He became a professor at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in 1766.

Dadd went to Greece, Turkey, Syria and Egypt in 1842 as the draughtsman for Sir Thomas Phillips. On the Nile he became delusional and believed the god Osiris had hold of him. Back in England he decided his father was the Devil in disguise and killed him with a knife. He was committed to Bethlem and later to Broadmoor. The doctors there encouraged him to paint. He spent from 1855 to 1864 on The Fairy Feller's Master-Stroke.

For years Thomas de Keyser was the portrait painter everyone in the Netherlands wanted, until Rembrandt took over in the 1630s. Later, some of his paintings were wrongly credited to Rembrandt. His father was the sculptor and architect Hendrik de Keyser, and the family lived on the Amsterdam canal Groenburgwal. In 1622 he joined the Guild of St. Luke with his brother Pieter. He also traded in bluestone and worked as a stone mason.

Michallon won the first Prix de Rome ever given for landscape painting, in 1817. His father and his uncle were both sculptors. He studied under Jacques-Louis David and Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes. He went to Italy in 1818 and stayed for more than two years. Then pneumonia killed him at 25. Whether the young Corot was his pupil is still disputed.

Valdés Leal painted death more than once. Two of his pictures, In ictu oculi and Finis gloriae mundi, were painted for the Charity Hospital in Seville. His friend Murillo painted in a peaceful, serene way, while Valdés Leal preferred somber and dramatic subjects. After he came back to Seville in 1656, the two founded the Seville Academy of Art. His wife Isabella Carasquilla was a painter too, and several of their five children became artists.

Raphaelle Peale is considered the first professional American painter of still life. His father, Charles Willson Peale, trained him. They collaborated on portraits, and on some commissions Raphaelle painted the miniatures while his brother Rembrandt did the full-size portraits. In 1793 he traveled to South America to collect specimens for his father's museum. He and Rembrandt tried to start a second museum in Charleston in 1797, but the plan fell through. He spent his life in Philadelphia and had eight children.

Frans Hals painted Hendrik Gerritsz Pot in his militia sash, and Pot is the man reading a book on the far right of that picture. Pot himself lived and painted in Haarlem, where he was an officer of the militia. He was probably a pupil of Karel van Mander, as Hals was, and the two influenced each other. In 1632 he went to London and painted King Charles I and Queen Henrietta Maria. Those portraits now hang in the Royal Collection. He served as dean of the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke three times.

Eva Gonzalès began as Manet's model and then became his student in 1869. Manet's portrait of her shows her at an easel in an expensive dress that is clearly unfit for painting. Her father was the writer Emmanuel Gonzalès, who introduced her to Paris literary and art circles early. She had her first lessons at sixteen with the society portraitist Charles Chaplin. She is named as one of the four most notable female Impressionists, along with Mary Cassatt, Berthe Morisot and Marie Bracquemond. She died in 1883.

Nobody knows the real name of Juan de Flandes. The Spanish name means John of Flanders. An inscription reading Juan Astrat on the back of one panel suggests Jan van der Straat, and Jan Sallaert has also been proposed. He probably trained in Ghent, since his work resembles that of Joos van Wassenhove and Hugo van der Goes. The first record of him is from 1496, when he was at the court of Queen Isabella of Castile. He painted portraits of her family and most of the small panels for an altarpiece she ordered.

La Tour made pastel portraits of Voltaire, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Louis XV and Madame de Pompadour. He was the third son of a musician from Saint-Quentin. He is popularly said to have had a father who disapproved of his career, but nothing supports that. At about nineteen he left for Paris after an indiscretion involving his cousin Anne Bougier, and by then he already called himself a painter. After a short trip to England in 1725 he returned to Paris in 1727, where he was encouraged to work as a portraitist in pastels.

Nicholson began in Pickering, painting sporting pictures and portraits for Yorkshire patrons. When he started painting country houses in the mid-1780s, he turned to landscapes in watercolour. From 1789 he sent views of Yorkshire and Scotland to the Royal Academy, and he supplied topographical views for the Copper Plate Magazine. His market became more and more London-based, but he lived in Whitby, Knaresborough and Ripon until about 1803. In 1804 he was a founder member of the Society of Painters in Watercolours. He also wrote a handbook on painting landscape from nature in watercolours.

Dauzats grew up in Bordeaux wanting to paint stage scenery, since his father was a scene painter at the city theatre. He studied with Lacour at the École de Dessin. Around 1829 he travelled with Baron Taylor, an archaeologist, to Egypt, Syria, Mount Sinai and Palestine to make illustrations for Taylor's travel books. After that trip he painted Oriental subjects, and he was one of the first artists to do so with scrupulous exactitude. At the Salon he showed genre scenes and church interiors.

William Hart's first artistic job was painting landscapes on the panels of coaches. He was born in Paisley, Scotland, and his family emigrated to Albany, New York, in 1831. A trip through Michigan in the late 1830s to find portrait commissions came to nothing. In 1849 Dr. James Armsby paid for him to study landscape painting in Europe, and he worked mostly in Scotland. He came back as a landscape painter, known for cattle. His brother James and his sister Julie Hart Beers were also Hudson River School artists.

Harry Fenn left London for the United States to see Niagara Falls, and he stayed. He had trained as a wood engraver with the Dalziel firm. His first big success was a set of pictures for John Greenleaf Whittier's poem Snow-Bound, published in 1867 for the Christmas trade. Its small images opened many eyes to what wood engraving could do. From 1870 to about 1895 he was the most prominent landscape illustrator in the country.

Ren Bonian, also called Ren Yi, was the son of a rice merchant who made extra money painting portraits. Born in Zhejiang, he moved to Shanghai after his father died in 1855. The city was open to Western ideas, and he joined the Shanghai School, which blended popular and traditional styles. He is counted with Ren Xiong, Ren Xun and Ren Yu as one of the Four Rens. He was noted for bold brushstrokes and use of colour. Early on he followed Song dynasty painters, but later he moved to a freer style in the manner of Zhu Da.

Robert Sayer sold prints, maps and sea charts near the Golden Buck at 53 Fleet Street in London. He started as the assistant of Mary Overton, a widow who married his brother James. By 1748 he was managing the shop, and he gradually took over the whole Overton business. A servant named John Bennett rose to become his partner with a one-third share. After Bennett was admitted to an asylum in 1781, Sayer tried to end the partnership in 1785. He also published atlases.

Gillis Mostaert ran a large workshop in Antwerp that supplied works to prominent patrons. His winter landscapes, fire scenes and night scenes were among the most sought-after pieces of his time. He was born in Hulst. Karel van Mander says he was the twin brother of the painter Frans Mostaert. Van Mander also says Gillis studied landscape painting with Jan Mandijn, but no guild record shows it. He often worked together with leading Antwerp artists.

Edward Francis Finden worked alongside his older brother William, who was also his fellow pupil, and the two shared their successes and fortunes. Much of his work went into annuals, books of beauty and poetry, the sentimental books then in vogue. He engraved The Harvest Waggon after Thomas Gainsborough and The Little Gleaner after Sir William Beechey. He also made engravings for the landscape painter James Duffield Harding. Finden died at St. John's Wood aged 65. He is buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Isakson drew his first pictures surrounded by piles of laundry. His father, a blacksmith, died when the boy was eight months old, and his mother raised him and his sister by running a laundry in Stockholm. At school he was known as the little professor. He left at 13 to work as a painter's assistant, and at 15 he started evening drawing classes on his own. He worked as Carl Larsson's assistant before entering the Swedish Academy. Much of his career was spent in Denmark, where he painted many pictures of Christiansø.

In 1878 Henrique Bernardelli took Brazilian nationality so he could compete for the academy's travel award to Europe. He lost it to Rodolfo Amoedo but went to Rome in 1879 on his own money. He was born in Valparaíso. His parents, a violinist and a dancer, were hired by Emperor Pedro II to tutor the imperial princesses, and his brothers were the sculptor Rodolfo and the painter and violinist Félix. At the Paris Universal Exhibition in 1889 his painting Os Bandeirantes won a bronze medal.

Wahl was among the first northern artists to paint portraits in the new French style, which stressed a sitter's rank rather than personality. He trained in Leipzig with the court painter David Hoyer and then settled in Hamburg as a portrait painter. The Danish royal family called him to Denmark in 1719. Christian VI made him court painter when he came to the throne. In 1737 Wahl took over running the Royal Collection. His portraits of people outside the nobility are freer in style.

John Michael Wright trained in Edinburgh under George Jamesone, although he was born and raised in London, and in documents he sometimes called himself Scottish. A long stay in Rome earned him a place in the Accademia di San Luca. In 1655 Archduke Leopold Wilhelm of Austria engaged him to acquire art in Cromwell's England. He settled in England the next year and served as court painter before and after the Restoration. A Catholic convert, he painted for both Charles II and James II. Late in life he went back to Rome with an embassy to Pope Innocent XI.

Robert Edge Pine held radical political opinions, and they likely kept him out of the founding group of the Royal Academy in 1768. He painted John Wilkes during the politician's imprisonment and exile. Pine was the son of the engraver John Pine and the uncle of the watercolourist John Robert Cozens. In London he moved in the circle of the anatomist William Hunter and painted Hunter and his sister. Some of his Shakespeare scenes later appeared in Boydell's Shakespeare. He spent his last four years in Philadelphia.

Andrea di Bartolo grew up in his father's workshop in Siena. Bartolo di Fredi was a very prominent painter there, and his son's hand may be visible in his work of the 1380s. In 1389 the two, along with Luca di Tommè, made an altarpiece for the shoemakers' guild altar in the cathedral. It is his first documented work, now lost. He probably opened his own workshop around 1390. His patrons came from the same circles as his father's, such as the Franciscans of Montalcino and the Dominicans of Siena.

At eleven Laermans caught meningitis, and it left him deaf and almost mute. Some sources say he was born deaf. Either way, his attention turned to sight, and he decided to become a painter. After he joined the Decadent movement in 1890 he illustrated Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du mal. By 1893 his pictures looked more like Bruegel's, and he had settled on his main subject, downtrodden laborers and poor peasants. The novel La Nouvelle Carthage by Georges Eekhoud inspired his triptych Emigrants, which he considered his best work.

Gavin Hamilton is remembered as much for hunting down antiquities near Rome as for his paintings. He was born in Lanarkshire and entered the University of Glasgow at 15. By 1744 he was in Italy, and from 1748 he shared an apartment with James Stuart, Matthew Brettingham and Nicholas Revett. After several years painting portraits in London he went back to Rome in 1756 and stayed there until he died. His most famous work is a cycle of six paintings from Homer's Iliad.

Michael Sittow came from Reval, now Tallinn in Estonia, where his father Clawes was a painter and wood-carver. He was the eldest of three brothers. He trained in the Early Netherlandish tradition. For most of his life he worked as a court portrait painter for Isabella of Castile and her Habsburg relatives. That took him to Spain and the Netherlands. He also painted for other royal houses, and his name appears in many forms, among them Master Michiel and Miguel Sithium.

Carlo Bianconi trained in Bologna with Ercole Graziani the Younger and made many engravings of antiquities. With Mauro Tesi he designed a monument to their patron, Count Francesco Algarotti. He belonged to the Accademia Clementina. In 1778 he moved to Milan, where he served as secretary of the Brera Academy for twenty years. He had helped edit Malvasia's guide to Bologna and in 1787 published his own guide to arts and antiquities in Milan. His brother Giovanni Ludovico was a doctor and art historian and a close friend of Winckelmann.

Coello's surname comes from the Portuguese word for rabbit. His parents were Portuguese, but he was born in Madrid and learned painting there from Francisco Rizi. While still in that school he made an altarpiece for San Plácido. A friendship with the court painter Juan Carreño de Miranda gave him access to the royal collection, where he studied Titian, Rubens and van Dyck. His best known work is in the sacristy of El Escorial, which holds portraits of priests and courtiers. He became court painter to Charles II.

Sarah Goodridge made her first sketches on birch bark because she could not afford paper. She was born in Templeton, Massachusetts, and was mostly self-taught, since women had few chances to study where she lived. In Boston she met Gilbert Stuart, who criticized her work and gave her lessons in technique. In 1825 she made a portrait of him that he called the only true likeness anyone had done of him. Her sister Elizabeth also painted miniatures. Her subjects included General Henry Lee and Theophilus Parsons.

Anna Boch bought The Red Vineyard, which is believed to be the only painting Vincent van Gogh sold in his lifetime. Van Gogh was a friend of her brother Eugène, who was a painter too. Anna was the only woman in the artistic group Les XX. She painted in an early Pointillist style, then spent most of her career as an Impressionist. Her collection also held works by Gauguin, Signac and James Ensor. Her father was a successful porcelain manufacturer.

Jacob Binck is counted as a peripheral member of the Little Masters group of engravers. He was born in Cologne and may have been a pupil of Dürer, though his early stay in Italy casts doubt on that. One of his biggest plates is a copy of Raphael's Massacre of the Innocents. Before 1546 he became painter to King Christian III of Denmark. In 1549 Prince Albrecht of Brandenburg sent him to the Netherlands to put up a monument, then gave him a fixed salary and took him to Königsberg.

Piero Benci is better known as Piero del Pollaiuolo. His brother Antonio, about ten years older, was seen by contemporaries as the greater talent. Antonio was also a sculptor, while Piero seems only to have painted. The brothers kept separate workshops in a shared building, which makes it hard to tell who painted what. Piero signed and dated just one picture, a Coronation of the Virgin of 1483 in San Gimignano. Art historians now give him more credit than Vasari did, and the National Gallery assigns its Apollo and Daphne to him.

Mariotto di Nardo was the son and apprentice of the painter Nardo di Cione and the grandson of Andrea di Cione. Nobody knows much about his own family, or whether he had one at all. He worked in Florence at the Duomo, at Santa Maria Maggiore and at Orsanmichele, making frescoes, panel paintings and manuscript illuminations. His style shows the influence of Spinello Aretino and Niccolò di Pietro Gerini, and later a little of Lorenzo Monaco. He joined the Company of Saint Luke in 1408. Documents suggest he was much sought after for both public and private work.

Thomas Waterman Wood got the idea for The Contraband, Recruit and Veteran from a one-legged Black man he saw in Louisville, hobbling along on homemade crutches. The painting is about the move from slavery to freedom, and it now belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Wood was born in Montpelier in Vermont and studied briefly in Boston with the portrait painter Chester Harding. He settled in New York City in 1866 as a figure painter. He became president of the American Water Color Society in 1878 and president of the National Academy of Design in 1891.

Pierre-Antoine Labouchère was intended for a commercial career and started out in business in Antwerp. He was born in Nantes. He then travelled to America, China and Italy and finally became a pupil of Paul Delaroche in Paris. Many of his subjects came from the Reformation, such as Charles V in London. He also did drawings for Merle d'Aubigné's life of Luther and painted a portrait of Guizot. In 1849 he stayed with his sister and her husband at Southrop Manor in Gloucestershire, where he painted Southrop House.

Ubu began as a joke at school. In Rennes, Jarry and his classmate Henri Morin wrote a marionette play about their obese, incompetent physics teacher, a blunderer called Père Heb. Heb later grew into Ubu in Ubu Roi, his best known play and one often cited as a forerunner of Dada and Surrealism. Jarry also coined the word pataphysics. His first collection, Les minutes de sable mémorial, came out in 1893. His mother died of influenza that year and his father two years later.

Daniel Dumonstier was nicknamed the best artist in crayons in Europe of his time, though he is little known now. He was born outside marriage and later legitimised. His father Cosme, his uncle Pierre and his cousin Pierre II were all artists as well. He drew portraits of major figures in 17th century France. Nobody knows if he painted too. In 2006 the musée Condé at Chantilly showed all 30 works known by him.

Isak Wacklin was the first professional artist in Finland, yet researchers have long found him a mystery. He was born in Oulu when Finland was under Swedish rule, the son of a postmaster. In 1743 he applied for a passport to St. Petersburg, where he could support his family, which he had not managed in Finland. Besides portraits, mostly from the late 1750s, he painted landscapes, as Nils Schillmark did. He was the only representative of Finnish rococo. He died in Stockholm at 38.

Marco Pino is also called Marco da Siena after the city where he first trained. He was born in Costalpino and later worked in Rome and in Naples, where he died. He is said to have been a pupil of Beccafumi and Daniele da Volterra. The biographer Filippo Baldinucci adds that he worked for Baldassare Peruzzi. In Messina his son-in-law Antonio Spanò learned from him. In Naples his pupils included Fabrizio Santafede.

Pierre Gobert painted the great ladies of Louis XIV's court, and he often gave them the traits of figures from mythology. One portrait shows Mademoiselle de Blois as a triumphant Galatea. He was born in Fontainebleau, the son of the sculptor Jean II Gobert. In 1701 he entered the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture as a portraitist. He died in 1744.

Pierre Parrocel came from a large family of artists in Avignon, among them his uncle Joseph and his father Louis. His uncle taught him first, and then he trained with Carlo Maratti in Rome. In 1730 he joined the Accademia di San Luca there. His main work was thirteen pictures telling the story of Tobit in the gallery of the Hôtel de Noailles at St. Germain-en-Laye. He also painted a Coronation of the Virgin in a church in Marseille. Fourteen etchings by him survive, among them The Triumph of Aphrodite.

Coccorante painted imaginary landscapes full of classical ruins, called capricci. He often put small figures in the foreground so the ruins looked even bigger. He was born in Naples and studied or worked under several painters, among them the Flemish landscape painter Jan Frans van Bloemen. From 1737 to 1739 he was employed decorating the royal palace of Naples. His paintings are in the Louvre and in museums in Milan, Trapani, Grenoble and Beauvais.

Leopolski was meant to be a lawyer and began studying law at the University of Lviv. After graduating he turned to art, studying painting in Krakow with Wojciech Korneli Stattler and Władysław Łuszczkiewicz, then in Vienna with Christian Ruben. In Vienna he made a thorough study of the Dutch and Venetian Old Masters. He moved on to the Munich academy to study with Alexander von Wagner. After he graduated in 1862 he went home to Brody, and he withdrew from public life during the January Uprising.

As a teenager Deming traveled in Oklahoma and sketched the Native people he met. He grew up in Geneseo, Illinois, where the Winnebago people were sometimes his family's neighbors. He studied at the Art Students League of New York and then at the Académie Julian in Paris. Then he spent two years painting cycloramas. He became known for pictures of Blackfeet people and wild animals. One of his murals was adapted for a US postage stamp.

Hans Maler painted almost every portrait in the same way: a bust, with the hands hidden and the eyes looking away from the viewer. He was born in Ulm and worked in Schwaz, a village near Innsbruck, and he may have trained with Bartholomäus Zeitblom. His two most important patrons were Ferdinand I of Austria, then still an archduke, and the Fugger family. Ferdinand ordered at least three portraits of himself and four of his wife, Anna of Bohemia and Hungary. In 1517 Maler painted Sebastian Andorfer, a metal maker and merchant from Schwaz.

Kanō Mitsunobu first appears in the records working with his father, Kanō Eitoku, on the painting of Azuchi Castle for Oda Nobunaga. Later they worked together on Osaka Castle and on Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Jurakudai palace. Toyotomi Hideyori had him paint dragons on the ceiling of the main hall of Shōkoku-ji in Kyoto. When Eitoku died in 1590, Mitsunobu became head of the family and the school. Weak leadership and political skills cost him commissions to the rival Hasegawa school and to siblings in his own school. Scholars cannot agree if he was born in 1561 or 1565.

Xu Daoning started out selling medicine prescriptions in Kaifeng. While he sold them, he also began painting nature scenes in the manner of Li Cheng. Once he became popular he took on murals for Chinese nobles. He lived under the Northern Song dynasty and came from Chang'an, now Xi'an, or from Hejian. His best known work is Fishermen's Evening Song, from around 1049. He died sometime in the early 1050s.

Battaglioli painted views and capriccios of Venice and the Venetian mainland, but he also worked in Spain. For Ferdinand VI he painted scenery sets for the theatre at the Palacio Real de Aranjuez. Two of them are in the Prado. There he worked with Farinelli on stage sets for operas by Pietro Metastasio, among them La Nitteti and Didone Abbandonata. In 1778 he succeeded Antonio Visentini as professor of perspective at the academy in Venice.

Valentijn Bing was the son of an Amsterdam merchant and his English wife. He studied under Jan Adam Kruseman and began showing his work at the Exhibition of Living Masters. From 1843 he taught at the academy, and his students included Jan Portielje and Marie Wandscheer. With a fellow lithographer he wrote and illustrated a book on the traditional costumes of the Netherlands. They also made two instructional books on drawing. He never married.

Tišov grew up in the village of Viškovci near Đakovo and went on to the School of Crafts in Zagreb. He studied in Vienna and then won a scholarship to the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. While still a student in Vienna he was commissioned to paint four allegories on the ceiling of the Golden Hall in Zagreb: worship, theology, art and science. His picture of Art, also called Music, won a bronze medal. From 1895 he taught at the Zagreb academy for the rest of his life.

Caula learned to paint in Modena from Jean Boulanger, then finished his studies in Venice by looking at the works of Titian and Tintoretto. Besides altarpieces he painted small cabinet pictures for private collections. His large picture of St Charles Borromeo helping the plague victims of Modena was made for the church of San Carlo, and it now hangs in the Este Gallery there. The gallery also has a St Ambrose by him. In his later years his colour and execution got more languid. He was still painting in 1694.

John Robert Cozens had a complete mental collapse at 42 and never recovered in the three years he had left. Before that he made two long trips to the Alps and Italy, sketching in line and grey wash. Back in London he worked the sketches up into watercolours, sometimes using the same sketch several times. His father, Alexander Cozens, taught him and was known as the Blotmaster for building landscapes from random blots of ink. Turner and Girtin copied many of John Robert's watercolours when young, paid by Dr Monro. Constable called him all poetry.

Israël Henriet grew up in Nancy as a childhood friend of Jacques Callot. The two studied engraving together in Florence under Antonio Tempesta. In Paris he made a living as a drawing master to wealthy families and the court, and he eventually taught Louis XIII. Prints became his main business once he settled there in 1622. After Callot died, Henriet acquired the exclusive rights to publish his etchings. His nephew Israel Silvestre lived in his house and inherited his stock of plates.

Pierre-Jacques Volaire was also called le chevalier Volaire. His father, Jacques, was the official city painter of Toulon and a writer. Volaire became a pupil of Claude-Joseph Vernet and then spent eight years as his assistant while Vernet painted the Ports of France series. How much he painted in that series is uncertain. He left for Rome in 1764 and settled in Naples five years later. He stayed there until he died, in 1799 or 1802.

Johan Cohen Gosschalk married Johanna Bonger, the widow of Theo van Gogh, in 1901. In 1905 he helped organize a Vincent van Gogh exhibition at the Stedelijk Museum and wrote the introduction to its catalogue. He had trained as a lawyer and took painting lessons from Jan Veth in Bussum. Most of his own works were portraits or landscapes, and he wrote about art for magazines. His health failed after 1910. After he died, Johanna put on a retrospective of his work.

Kanō Naonobu was the younger brother of Kanō Tan'yū, and the two completed several large commissions for the Tokugawa shogunate. He was the second son of the painter Kanō Takanobu and was born in Kyoto. The shogunate invited him to Edo in 1630, where he set up at the Takekawa workshop. He studied under his brother and under a lesser known Kanō artist, Kanō Kō-i. His style was different from Tan'yū's, with bold negative space and a skilled hand with ink wash. He also used the art name Jitekisai.

Étienne-Louis Boullée designed private houses in Paris between 1762 and 1778, and most are gone. The Hôtel de Brunoy was demolished in 1930, but the Hôtel Alexandre survives. He studied under Jacques-François Blondel. He became chief architect to Frederick II of Prussia, a largely honorary title. His biggest impact came as a teacher and theorist at the École Nationale des Ponts et Chaussées. He stripped away ornament and blew up geometric forms to a huge scale.

Felsing learned the elements of engraving in Darmstadt. He had been born in Giessen and engraved many portraits in the dotted manner. Topographical works distinguished him more, and the last and best of them was a military plan of Mayence in 1815. He died in Darmstadt in 1819. His son Georg Jakob Felsing became an eminent engraver, and another son, Johann Heinrich, was a celebrated copper-plate printer.
